'''''Leucanthemum vulgare''''', commonly known as the '''ox-eye daisy''', '''oxeye daisy''', '''dog daisy''', '''marguerite''' ({{langx|fr|Marguerite commune}}, "common marguerite") and other common names,<ref name="RBGS" /> is a widespread [[flowering plant]] native to [[Europe]] and the temperate regions of [[Asia]], and an introduced plant to [[North America]], [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]].

==Description==
''L. vulgare'' is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] that grows to a height of {{convert|80|cm|abbr=off}}<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/383/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |page=383 |orig-date=1979}}</ref> and has a creeping underground [[rhizome]]. The lower parts of the stem are hairy, sometimes densely hairy but more or less [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]] in the lower parts. The largest leaves are at the base of the plant and are {{cvt|4–15|cm|frac=4}} long, about {{cvt|5|cm|frac=4}} wide and have a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]. These leaves have up to 15 teeth, or lobes or both on the edges. The leaves decrease in size up the stem, the upper leaves up to {{cvt|7.5|cm|frac=4}} long, lack a petiole and are deeply toothed.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Qld">{{cite web |title=''Leucanthemum vulgare'' |url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/leucanthemum_vulgare.htm |publisher=Queensland Government Weeds of Australia |access-date=22 January 2019}}</ref><ref name="Muelleria">{{cite journal |last1=Thompson |first1=Ian R. |title=A taxonomic treatment of tribe Anthemidae (Asteracea) in Australia |journal=Muelleria |date=2007 |volume=25 |pages=39–40 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/279546#page/41/mode/1up |access-date=25 November 2023}}</ref><ref name="OEH" /><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Walsh |first1=Neville|author-link1=Neville Grant Walsh |title=''Leucanthemum vulgare'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/f53fe9e2-63f8-440d-9e3b-58dd52e3a8f4 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=23 January 2019}}</ref>

The plant bears up to three "flowers" like those of a typical [[Asteraceae|daisy]]. Each is a "head" or [[Pseudanthium|capitulum]] {{cvt|2–7.5|cm|frac=8}} wide.<ref name=":0" /> Each head has between fifteen and forty white "petals" ([[ray floret]]s) {{convert|1–2|cm|frac=8}} long surrounding the yellow disc florets. Below the head is an involucre of glabrous green [[bract]]s {{convert|7–10|mm|abbr=off|frac=8}} long with brownish edges. Flowering occurs from May to October.<ref name=":0" /> The seed-like [[achene]]s are {{cvt|1–3|mm|frac=16}} long and have ten "ribs" along their edges but lack a [[Pappus (botany)|pappus]].<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Brown |first1=Elizabeth A. |title=''Leucanthemum vulgare'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Leucanthemum~vulgare |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=23 January 2019}}</ref><ref name="Qld" /><ref name="Muelleria" />

Ox-eye daisy is similar to shasta daisy ([[Leucanthemum × superbum|''Leucanthemum'' × ''superbum'']]) which has larger flower heads ({{cvt|5–12|cm|disp=or|frac=8}} wide) and to stinking chamomile (''[[Anthemis cotula]]'') which has smaller heads ({{cvt|1.5–3|cm|disp=or|frac=8}} wide).<ref name="Qld" /> ''[[Leucanthemum maximum|L. maximum]]'' is also similar, usually with rays {{Convert|2-3|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} in length.<ref name=":0" />

==Taxonomy==
''L. vulgare'' was first formally described in 1778 by [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]], who published the description in ''Flore françoise''.<ref name="TPL" /><ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Leucanthemum vulgare''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/507504|publisher=APNI|access-date=22 January 2019}}</ref><ref name="Lam.">{{cite book |last1=Lamarck |first1=Jean-Baptiste |title=Flore françoise (Volume 2) |date=1778 |volume=2 |location=Paris |page=137 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/38207#page/144/mode/1up |access-date=22 January 2019|publisher=l'Imprimerie Royale }}</ref> It is also known by the common names ox-eye daisy, dog daisy, field daisy, Marguerite, moon daisy, moon-penny, poor-land penny, poverty daisy and white daisy.<ref name="RBGS" />

The species was formerly described as part of the ''[[Chrysanthemum]]'' genus.<ref name=":0" />

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:024 065 Ile Madeleine.jpg|thumb|''Leucanthemum'' L.,<ref name="Leucanthemum L florelauremtienne.com">{{cite web |author1=Frère Marie-Victorin |title=Leucanthemum Linné. ― Leucanthème. ― Marguerite. ― (Ox-eye daisy). |url=https://florelaurentienne.com/flore/Groupes/Spermatophytes/Angiospermes/Dicotyles/103Composees/32_Chrysanthemum/leucanthemum.htm |publisher=florelaurentienne.com |access-date=19 March 2024 |date=2001-10-23 |quote=The folklore of this species is abundant and well known: young men and women pluck the leaves of a daisy to find out the truth about their love affairs}}</ref> field in [[Les Îles-de-la-Madeleine, Quebec|Magdalen Island]], Canada]]
The species is native to [[Europe]], and to [[Turkey]] and [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] in [[Western Asia]]. It is a typical [[grassland]] perennial [[wildflower]], growing in a variety of [[plant community|plant communities]] including [[meadows]] and [[Field (agriculture)|field]]s, under [[Shrubland|scrub]] and open-canopy forests, and in disturbed areas. The species is widely [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in many parts of the world, including [[North America]],<ref name=":0" /> and is considered to be an [[invasive species]] in more than forty countries. It grows in temperate regions where average annual rainfall exceeds {{cvt|750|mm}}, and often where soils are heavy and damp. It is often a weed of degraded pastures and roadsides.<ref name="Qld" /><ref name="OEH">{{cite web |title=Ox-eye daisy |date=29 June 2018 |url=https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/topics/animals-and-plants/pest-animals-and-weeds/weeds/widespread-weeds/ox-eye-daisy |publisher=New South Wales Government Office of Environment and Heritage |access-date=22 January 2019}}</ref><ref name="cirrusweed">{{cite web|url=http://www.cirrusimage.com/flower_ox-eye_daisy.htm|title=Ox-Eye Daisy – ''Chrysanthemum leucanthemum''|work=cirrusimage.com}}</ref><ref name="Vic">{{cite web |title=Ox-eye daisy (''Leucanthemum vulgare'') |url=http://vro.agriculture.vic.gov.au/dpi/vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/weeds_herbs_perennial_ox_eye_daisy# |publisher=State of Victoria (Agriculture Victoria) |access-date=22 January 2019}}</ref><ref name="NWCB">{{cite web |title=Oxeye daisy ''Leucanthemum vulgare'' |url=https://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weeds/oxeye-daisy |publisher=Washington State Weed Control Board |access-date=22 January 2019}}</ref>

==Ecology==
The species spreads by seeds and by shallow, creeping [[rhizome]]s. A mature plant can produce up to 26,000 seeds that are spread by animals, vehicles, water and contaminated agricultural produce, and some seeds remain viable for up to nearly forty years. It is not palatable to cattle and reduces the amount of quality pasture available for grazing. In native landscapes such as the [[Kosciuszko National Park]] in Australia, dense infestation can exclude native plants, causing soil erosion and loss of soil organic matter.<ref name="Qld" /><ref name="OEH" /><ref name="Vic" /><ref name="NWCB" />

This plant was top-ranked for pollen production per floral unit sampled at the level of the entire capitulum, with a value of 15.9 ± 2 μL, in a [[United Kingdom|UK]] study of meadow flowers.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hicks|first1=DM|last2=Ouvrard|first2=P|last3=Baldock|first3=KCR|title=Food for Pollinators: Quantifying the Nectar and Pollen Resources of Urban Flower Meadows|journal=PLOS ONE |volume=11 |issue=6|date=2016|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0158117|pmc=4920406|pmid=27341588|article-number=e0158117|bibcode=2016PLoSO..1158117H|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===As an invasive species===
[[File:Leucanthemum vulgare infestation.jpg|thumb|Infestation in native pasture near [[Guyra, New South Wales|Guyra]] in Australia]]

''L. vulgare'' is one of the most widespread weeds in the [[Anthemideae]]. It became an [[introduced species]] via gardens into [[Natural environment|natural area]]s in parts of [[Canada]],<ref name=ROM>{{cite book |author1=T. Dickinson |author2=D. Metsger |author3=J. Bull |author4=R. Dickinson |year=2004 |title=ROM Field Guide to Wildflowers of Ontario |location=Toronto |publisher=[[Royal Ontario Museum]] |page=175}}</ref> the [[United States]],<ref name=invasive>[http://www.invasive.org/browse/subinfo.cfm?sub=5937 oxeye daisy, ''Leucanthemum vulgare'' (Asterales: Asteraceae)]. Invasive.org (2010-05-04). Retrieved on 2015-07-08.</ref> [[Australia]],<ref name="Qld" /> and [[New Zealand]].<ref name="NZ">{{cite web |title=Oxeye daisy |url=http://www.massey.ac.nz/massey/learning/colleges/college-of-sciences/clinics-and-services/weeds-database/oxeye-daisy.cfm |publisher=Massey University; University of New Zealand |access-date=23 January 2019}}</ref> In some [[habitat]]s it forms dense colonies displacing [[native plant]]s and modifying existing communities.<ref name="cirrusweed"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=LEVU|title=Plants Profile for ''Leucanthemum vulgare'' (oxeye daisy)|work=usda.gov}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?609,1555,1557|title=UC/JEPS: Jepson Manual treatment for LEUCANTHEMUM vulgare|work=berkeley.edu}}</ref>

The plant commonly invades [[lawn]]s, and is difficult to control or eradicate, since a new plant can regenerate from rhizome fragments<ref name="cirrusweed"/> and is a problem in pastures where beef and dairy cattle graze, as usually they will not eat it, thus enabling it to spread;<ref name="NZ" /> cows who do eat it produce milk with an undesirable flavor.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Reiner|first=Ralph E.|title=Introducing the Flowering Beauty of Glacier National Park and the Majestic High Rockies|publisher=Glacier Park, Inc.|year=1969|page=22}}</ref> It has been shown to carry several crop diseases.<ref name="IPA">{{cite web |title=''Leucanthemum vulgare'' |url=https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.html?sub=5937 |publisher=University of Georgia: Invasive plant atlas |access-date=23 January 2019}}</ref>

This species has been declared an environmental weed in [[New South Wales]] and [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]]. In New South Wales it grows from [[Glen Innes, New South Wales|Glen Innes]] on the [[Northern Tablelands]] to [[Bombala, New South Wales|Bombala]] in the far southeast of the state, and there are significant populations in the Kosciuszko National Park where it has invaded subalpine grassland, snowgum (''[[Eucalyptus pauciflora]]'') woodland and wetlands. In Victoria it is a prohibited species and must be eradicated or controlled.<ref name="Qld" /><ref name="DPI">{{cite web |title=Ox-eye daisy (''Leucanthemum vulgare'') |url=https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/Details/356 |publisher=New South Wales Government Department of Primary Industries |access-date=23 January 2019}}</ref>

==Uses==
===Food===
The unopened flower [[bud]]s can be [[marinate]]d and used in a similar way to [[caper]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wildfoods.ca/products-vegetables-ox-eyedaisycapers.html|title=Forbes Wild Food|work=wildfoods.ca|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070313114129/http://www.wildfoods.ca/products-vegetables-ox-eyedaisycapers.html|archive-date=2007-03-13}}</ref>

[[Maud Grieve]]'s ''Modern Herbal'' (1931) states that "The taste of the dried herb is bitter and tingling, and the odour faintly resembles that of [[Valerian (herb)|valerian]]."<ref name="Grieve">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FgW4KJUSXkIC&pg=PA248|page=248|title=A Modern Herbal: The Medicinal, Culinary, Cosmetic and Economic Properties, Cultivation and Folk-lore of Herbs, Grasses, Fungi, Shrubs, & Trees with All Their Modern Scientific Uses, Volume 1|author=Grieve, Maud|year=1971|publisher=Courier Corporation |author-link=Maud Grieve|isbn=978-0-486-22798-6}}</ref>

===Tea===
{{Citation needed span|text=Oxeye grows wild in the Arab Valley in Southern Palestine, where the flowers are picked and dried and used by Palestinians to make a local variety of herbal tea.|date=October 2025}}

=== Use in horticulture ===
''L. vulgare'' is widely cultivated and available as a perennial flowering [[ornamental plant]] for gardens and designed meadow [[designed landscape|landscape]]s. It thrives in a wide range of conditions but prefers a sunny or part-sun location of average soil that is damp (like many in the daisy family). The plant does well in raised and mulched garden beds that retain moisture and prevent weeds. It is a [[mesophyte]] and therefore requires more or less a continuous water supply.  The heads of faded and old blooms are often [[Deadheading (flowers)|deadheaded]] to promote further blooming and to maintain the appearance of the plant. There are [[cultivar]]s, such as 'May Queen', that begin blooming in early spring.{{Citation needed|date=June 2020}}

==Allergies==
Allergies to daisies do occur, usually causing [[contact dermatitis]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=Lynette A. Gordon |year=1999 |title=''Compositae dermatitis'' |journal=Australasian Journal of Dermatology |volume=40 |issue=3 |pages=123–130 |doi=10.1046/j.1440-0960.1999.00341.x |pmid=10439521|s2cid=6212252 }}</ref>

==Symbolism==
Since 1987 the daisy, specifically either oxeye daisy or the [[marguerite daisy]] (''Argyranthemum frutescens''), replaced [[red clover]] (''Trifolium pratense'') as the [[Floral emblem|national flower]] of [[Denmark]]. Over time oxeye daisy has become more popular as it is native to Denmark, in contrast to the marguerite daisy.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://naturstyrelsen.dk/om-os/kontakt/faq/nationalplanter-og-dyr/ |title=Nationalplanter og -dyr | publisher=Naturstyrelsen, Danish Ministry of the Environment |access-date=28 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321144950/https://naturstyrelsen.dk/om-os/kontakt/faq/nationalplanter-og-dyr/ |archive-date=21 March 2023 |language=da |trans-title=Nationalplants and -animals }}</ref>

It is also a [[National symbols of Latvia|popular symbol of Latvia]]. In an open vote by the botanical society in 1994 it was selected as the national flower.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cukura |first1=Ināra |date=15 May 2024 |title=Latvijas nacionālie simboli |url=https://enciklopedija.lv/skirklis/5068-Latvijas-nacion%C4%81lie-simboli |trans-title=Latvian national symbols |website=Nacionālā enciklopēdija |trans-website=National Encyclopedia |language=lv |publisher=Latvijas Nacionālā bibliotēka [National Library of Latvia] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240619203546/https://enciklopedija.lv/skirklis/5068-Latvijas-nacion%C4%81lie-simboli |archive-date=19 June 2024 |access-date=5 January 2025}}</ref>
